sections.html:
Kershaw County lies in north-central South Carolina within the Columbia metro area. Camden is the seat and the largest town, and Lugoff, Elgin, Kershaw, Liberty Hill, Westville and Cassatt round out the named places. Interstate 20 passes through, as do U.S. 1, 521 and 601.

Residents numbered 65,403 in the 2020 census, compared with 61,697 in 2010, and the estimate for 2025 is 73,166. Roughly 52.8 percent live in rural areas. A property here might be a town lot in Camden or several acres out toward Lake Wateree. Camden's age shows up in old lots and old deeds too, so an inherited house there can send a title search back through several owners.

Property tax in Kershaw County is split among three offices in the Kershaw County Government Center, Camden.

OfficeRoomWhat it handles
Assessor100Values real property and mobile homes, measures new construction, takes value appeals, processes 4 percent legal residence and agricultural applications
Auditor120Homestead exemptions
Treasurer140Collects real and personal taxes and fees, issues motor vehicle decals
  • The Treasurer's number is (803) 425-1529.
  • For delinquent accounts, dial the same number and ask for extension 4, the Delinquent Tax Collector.
  • Phone the Assessor to find out its hours before driving over.

Because all three are under one roof, one visit can settle a payoff, a legal residence question and a homestead check, as long as you have your parcel information with you.

After the due date, state law attaches a penalty, adds more in February and March, and eventually authorizes an execution. The schedule is in Section 12-45-180. Since the amount changes on those dates, ask the Treasurer for this year's figures before you build a closing date around them.

Property is reassessed on the state's five-year cycle. An owner is entitled to a notice whenever value or classification moves by $1,000 or more, so open any letter from the Assessor promptly.

The first move is a letter to the Assessor, sent within 90 days of the date the notice was mailed. A year with no notice leaves the door open: you may write at any time, and a letter that arrives before the first penalty date counts toward the current tax year.

What follows is a chain of short deadlines. Expect a conference within 30 days of your request, or as soon as practical. Your written protest follows, due 30 days after the meeting, and a written response usually arrives in another 30. Reaching the county Board of Assessment Appeals takes a filing within 30 days of that response. The last rung is a contested case hearing in the Administrative Law Court, which you request within 30 days of the Board's written decision.

A case that is unfinished on December 31 is billed at 80 percent of the protested amount, with the Assessor instructing the auditor. Interest covers the difference once the case ends. Sections 12-60-2510 to 12-60-2550 cover all of it. A notice about the reassessment appeal deadline also appears on the county's home page. Call the Assessor to confirm the window.

A home you live in is assessed at 4 percent of fair market value, covering up to five contiguous acres, where other property is at 6 percent. File by the first penalty date of the first year you want the rate. Rent the house out for more than 72 days in a calendar year and you lose it.

Your buyer must file a fresh application, because the status does not transfer. Section 12-43-220 penalizes a wrongly held rate at 100 percent of the tax. Farmland may qualify for 4 percent in some situations, and changing how it is used brings rollback taxes covering the current year and the three before. Chapter 43 of Title 12 has the rules.

Every $500 of value carries a $1.85 deed fee, divided $1.30 to the state and $0.55 to the county. The seller is generally the one on the hook for it.

Exemptions cover a deed returned to a lender by foreclosure or deed in lieu, and a quitclaim deed that merely confirms title for no payment. Title 12, Chapter 24 lists the exemptions. Phone the office that records your deed for its fee schedule and form requirements.

sections.h2: Acreage, inherited homes and older houses
sections.html:
Land that has been farmed or timbered deserves a call to the Assessor before you split or sell it. Agricultural classification and rollback taxes can produce back charges that a buyer will want settled at closing.

For an inherited house, the estate often has to be opened before a clean deed can be signed. That step, more than any other, holds up closings on family property. If a house has sat vacant, expect a buyer's inspector to look hard at the roof, the plumbing and the electrical system, and consider asking the county planning office and your insurer about anything that could come up.

sections.h2: Selling when taxes or title are a problem
sections.html:
Selling with an open tax account is workable. Most sellers go in this order.

  1. Call the Treasurer for a payoff. A delinquent account is the Delinquent Tax Collector's, at extension 4.
  2. Ask the Assessor if the parcel carries 4 percent status or an agricultural classification.
  3. Ask the Auditor if a homestead exemption sits on the account.
  4. Pass the payoff to the title company, and it pays the county from your proceeds while recording the deed.

Cash Home Buyers will make an offer on a Kershaw County house in its present condition, even with back taxes, a delinquent account or a tenant living there, and explain how the sale would proceed. A cash deal skips the lender's appraisal, so timing rests on title work and the payoff.

Bring a photo ID, the newest tax bill and the parcel number to the counter, and file the payoff letter with your closing papers.

Selling right after a reassessment notice? Find out from the Assessor if your appeal window is still open, and let the buyer know about any pending appeal so the next bill holds no surprises.

sections.h2: Dates and steps in a typical sale
sections.html:
A Kershaw County sale usually moves in four stages. First, the title company opens the file and orders the title search, which can run long for an old Camden lot. Second, the payoff is requested from the Treasurer so the county is paid at closing. Third, any open question with the Assessor, such as legal residence status or agricultural classification, is cleared up. Fourth, the deed is signed and recorded, and the deed fee is figured from the value.

The title search is the slowest piece for old lots, and an estate that was never opened is the most common cause of delay. If either applies to you, begin there before anything else. Both buyers and sellers do better with a list of every open item in hand a few weeks before the closing date.

faqs.q: Where is property tax paid in Kershaw County?
faqs.a: At the Treasurer, Room 140 of the Kershaw County Government Center in Camden, or through the payment link on the Treasurer's page. The phone is (803) 425-1529.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Kershaw County assessment?
faqs.a: A written objection is due 90 days after the notice is mailed. Once the Assessor replies, 30 days remain to reach the Board of Assessment Appeals.

faqs.q: Which office grants the homestead exemption in Kershaw County?
faqs.a: The Auditor, Room 120. The Assessor takes the 4 percent legal residence and agricultural applications.

faqs.q: How frequently is Kershaw County property reassessed?
faqs.a: On a five-year cycle, as the SC Department of Revenue requires. A notice is also required when value or classification changes by $1,000 or more.

faqs.q: If I sell my Kershaw County house, who pays the year's tax?
faqs.a: Normally it comes from your proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff, and tell your buyer to file their own legal residence application.
